title: dlgskill
text:
Workflow. Start with summary_dlg unless reading the full dialog, then find_msgs or view_dlg(incl_out=True) for code, prose, and outputs. Before editing, read nbdev.skill and exhash.skill; for cross-notebook searches, read rgapi.skill (nbrg).
Use message operations for dialogs and fastcore.nbio.Notebook/NbCell operations for plain notebooks. Diagnose with validate_nb, validate_cell, or read_nb. Raw text is only for unparseable files. Propose missing structural operations; never splice notebook JSON.
View fresh lnhashview_msg/lnhashview_cell addresses before hash-verified edits. Use plain msg_* editors where exhash cannot express the operation. Use structural find_msgs predicates for Python symbols/ASTs. Read neighboring prose, including with ids=.
Call documented APIs without speculative fallbacks. Display results bare, never slice or reformat their reprs. Review returned diffs and call dlg.validate().
Files and held objects. File functions take dlg=path, defaulting to set_dlg(path). Each call rereads; edits save automatically. Methods edit held objects until dlg.save(). Save before switching to file functions; reopen before resuming methods. Drop address arguments: msg_str_replace(id, ..., dlg=p) becomes m.str_replace(...). Use d.mk_message/d.remove_msgs in memory. Dialog(msgs) wraps a message list; m.dlg retains ownership.
Views and identity. Summaries use id:t[directives]:content: c=code, n=note, p=prompt, r=raw. Replies follow >; truncations end with a bracketed missing-character count. Directives are nbdev metadata, as in nbio summaries. XML uses item2xml, <out> replies, and directive attributes such as bare export.
File searches return MsgRows/MsgRow snapshots (id, msg_type, content, out, meta); method searches return live FoundMsgs. Index by exact id or unique prefix, never position. Context rows use - instead of the first :. Default context is one neighbor each side, including with ids=; headers_only defaults to zero.
Placement and metadata. The host calls set_cur_msg; writes never move it. Unanchored adds follow it, or append if unset/missing. Chain explicit after= anchors for successive additions.
m.exported and only_exp include source and metadata directives; assignable m.meta_exported uses metadata only. Message.update/update_msg replace attributes, including whole meta; mergemeta deep-merges, with None deleting keys. export=True adds and False removes, migrating source export to metadata without a negative directive. Diffs show XML and meta:. Text editors’ out=True edits prompt replies only; assign other outputs through m.output.
Kernel execution. %nbrun runs in the current kernel. Dialog.execute/Message.execute capture outputs on held messages and return RunResult (abbreviated successes, exceptions on failure). They block; use asyncio.to_thread in async hosts. Read Dialog.execute for selection, shell lifetime, and saving.
%%add_msg [dlg] [msg_type] [export] [before=<id>|after=<id>] takes an unquoted body, trimming trailing newlines. Keywords override bare tokens.
%nbrun [IDS/FLAGS] [fname=PATH] accepts above, below, all, exported, ignore_eval, continue_on_error, and show. fname overrides set_dlg; no selection runs all participating code cells. Only explicit ids display outputs unless show. Errors always name the cell; the final nbrun: N cells ok includes any failure count. Execution uses the kernel’s namespace and standard output/error handling. The magic returns a coroutine for the host to await.

set_dlg
def set_dlg(
    fname, # ipynb path that later calls will default to
    cls:NoneType=None, # `Dialog` subclass to read with from now on (None: keep current; initially `Dialog`)
):
Set the current dialog file, used by these functions when dlg is None


A host calls set_dlg to set the current file and set_cur_msg to set the current message within it. Solveit sets the message when running it. An add_msg call without explicit placement then inserts after the prompt receiving the answer. Writes never move the current message. Calling set_dlg clears it because message ids belong to a file. An unset or deleted current message makes add_msg append instead.
Pass cls to set_dlg to choose the Dialog subclass for subsequent file reads. A host can use this subclass with its own message fields from meta_attrs. The class setting survives later set_dlg calls until you replace it, including when switching files.
set_dlg expands ~ and resolves an absolute path immediately. Changing directories, including with %cd, does not change the current file.
You can read the stored id and path as dlgskill.cur_msgid and dlgskill.cur_dlg_path. Do not import these attributes with from ... import. The setters rebind them, which leaves an imported binding with an old value. For this reason, __all__ does not include them.


source

Dialog.msg
def msg(
    id, # A `Message` (matched by its id), or an id: exact, or unique prefix
):
The matching Message in this dialog


msg accepts a message object, an exact id, or a unique id prefix. Use the id stored in the notebook. It does not remove host display prefixes such as Solveit’s leading underscore.
The examples use a temporary dialog file. File-based calls will read it again on each call:

tdir = Path(mkdtemp())
d = Dialog(name='demo')
setup = d.mk_message('# Setup', msg_type=snote)
calc = d.mk_message('x = 21\nx*2', msg_type=scode, output=code_output('42'))
ask = d.mk_message('Double it.', msg_type=sprompt, output='It is **42**.')
bad = d.mk_message('1/0', msg_type=scode, output=[dict(output_type='error', ename='E', evalue='boom', traceback=['tb'])])
write_ipynb(d, tdir/'demo.ipynb')
test_eq(d.msg(calc.id), calc)
test_eq(d.msg(calc.id[:5]), calc)  # unique prefixes work too
with expect_fail(KeyError, 'no message'): d.msg('zzzz')

A search result can include both matches and the messages that explain them. find_msgs includes one neighbor on each side by default, even when filtering by ids.
Index results with a message id or unique prefix that you read from the result. Integer indexing raises an error: position zero could contain context rather than the match you wanted. Missing or ambiguous ids also raise errors.

def find_msgs(
    re_pattern:str='', # Regex over content (a prompt's reply included), DOTALL+MULTILINE; an invalid regex matches literally
    msg_type:str=None, # Optional limit by type ('code', 'note', 'prompt', or 'raw')
    only_err:bool=False, # Only code messages with error outputs?
    only_exp:bool=False, # Only exported messages (nbdev export directive in content or meta)?
    ids:str='', # Optionally filter by ids (comma-separated str, or list); results are always in dialog order, whatever order the ids are given
    before:int=0, # Also include n messages before each match
    after:int=0, # Also include n messages after each match
    context:int=None, # Messages of context around matches (default 1, or 0 when `headers_only`)
    limit:int=None, # Max matched messages
    use_case:bool=False, # Case-sensitive matching?
    use_regex:bool=True, # Regex matching (else plain substring)?
    headers_only:bool=False, # Only heading notes (an outline view)?
    header_section:str=None, # Return the section starting with this heading, plus its children
    pred:<built-in function callable>=None, # Extra match criterion, e.g. from `symdef_finder`/`symref_finder`/`ast_finder`, or host-specific flags
)->__main__.FoundMsgs: # Live messages plus context rows, indexed by id, so results can be edited directly
Find this dialog’s messages matching all the given criteria


Dialog.find_msgs returns live messages. Edits through its result change the held dialog. You can search an existing message list by wrapping it in Dialog without changing the messages’ owners.
Search text matches a prompt’s request or reply. An invalid regular expression falls back to literal matching, allowing search text from users to include characters such as *. Pass pred for another criterion, such as a host-specific flag.
Use header_section for a section beginning at a note heading. Use headers_only for an outline. Outline searches default to no context. Other searches default to one message on each side. Pass context=0 for exact matches only:

test_eq(d.find_msgs('42', context=0), [ask])  # matches the reply text
test_eq(d.find_msgs(r'x\*2', msg_type=scode, context=0), [calc])
test_eq(d.find_msgs(only_err=True, context=0), [bad])
test_eq(len(d.find_msgs(r'x\*2')), 3)  # context defaults to 1: the match plus both neighbours
test_eq(d.find_msgs(headers_only=True), [setup])
test_eq(d.find_msgs(header_section='Setup', context=0), list(d.messages))  # everything under the heading
test_eq(Dialog(d.messages[:3]).find_msgs('42', context=0), [ask])  # an ephemeral wrap makes any message list searchable
fm = d.find_msgs('42', context=0)
fm[ask.id].content = 'Double it, please.'
test_eq(ask.content, 'Double it, please.')  # live objects: the edit landed on the dialog
assert ask.dlg is d  # ...and the wrap above didn't steal the message from its real dialog
test_eq(d.find_msgs('*42*', context=0), [ask])  # an invalid regex falls back to a literal match
test_eq(d.find_msgs(pred=lambda m: m.msg_type==sprompt, context=0), [ask])  # host-specific extra criterion
xd = Dialog(name='exports')
exp1 = xd.mk_message('#| export\ndef f(): pass', msg_type=scode)
exp2 = xd.mk_message('def g(): pass', msg_type=scode)
exp2.meta_exported = True
deep = xd.mk_message('## Deep\nbody under the heading', msg_type=snote)
test_eq(xd.find_msgs(only_exp=True, context=0), [exp1, exp2])
test_eq(xd.find_msgs(header_section='Deep', context=0), [deep])  # matched on the first line only
test_eq(xd.find_msgs(header_section='## Deep', context=0), [deep])  # a '#'-prefixed argument pins the level
test_eq(xd.find_msgs(header_section='# Deep', context=0), [])

A query by ids still includes neighboring messages. The integer-indexing error suggests an id from the actual matches:

fm = d.find_msgs(ids=calc.id)
test_eq((fm.matched, len(fm)), ({calc.id}, 3))
with expect_fail(TypeError, 'context rows'): fm[0]
test_eq(fm[calc.id], calc)
fm

1b68e089:c:x = 21¶x*2 ⇒ out(103)

> It is **42**.

rows = find_msgs('42', dlg=tdir/'demo.ipynb', context=0)
test_eq([r.id for r in rows], [ask.id])

assert not isinstance(rows[ask.id], Message) and rows[ask.id].msg_type==sprompt

Message.split
def split(
    *linenos:int, # Split before each of these 1-based lines
):
Split this message into pieces (returned as Msgs; the first keeps its id): one '\n\n' is absorbed at each cut (so merge_msgs restores blank-line-separated content byte-exactly), meta_attrs fields, the cell meta, and a leading #| export copy to every piece, attachments follow their references, and unreferenced ones stay on the first piece



sd = Dialog(name='s')
sm = sd.mk_message('#| export\ndef f(): pass\ndef g(): pass', msg_type=scode, meta={'k': 1})
i1,i2 = sm.split(3)
test_eq([m.content for m in sd.messages], ['#| export\ndef f(): pass', '#| export\ndef g(): pass'])
test_eq([m.meta for m in sd.messages], [{'k': 1}, {'k': 1}])  # whole cell meta copies to every piece
i2.meta['k'] = 2  # pieces don't share the dict
test_eq(i1.meta, {'k': 1})
sd.merge_msgs(i1, i2)
test_eq((sd.messages[0].content, sd.messages[0].meta), ('#| export\ndef f(): pass\n\ndef g(): pass', {'k': 1}))
hd = Dialog(name='hoist')
h1, h2 = hd.mk_message('def a(): pass'), hd.mk_message('#| export\ndef b(): pass')
hm = hd.merge_msgs(h1, h2)  # any exported piece exports the merge, via meta
test_eq((hm.content, hm.meta, hm.exported), ('def a(): pass\n\ndef b(): pass', {'nbdev': {'export': 'true'}}, True))
sd.mk_message('tail', msg_type=snote)
sd.move_msgs(i1, after=sd.messages[-1])
test_eq([m.content[:4] for m in sd.messages], ['tail', '#| e'])


ad = Dialog(name='atts')
at1, at2 = Attachment(b'x', 'text/plain'), Attachment(b'y', 'text/plain')
am = ad.mk_message(f'see attachment:{at1.id}\nplain tail', msg_type=snote, attachments=[at1, at2])
p1, p2 = am.split(2)
test_eq(len(p1.attachments), 2)  # the referenced one, plus the unreferenced one kept on the first piece
test_eq(p2.attachments, [])
jd = Dialog(name='junction')
j = jd.mk_message('a\n\n\nb', msg_type=snote)
j1, j2 = j.split(4)
test_eq((j1.content, j2.content), ('a\n', 'b'))  # one '\n\n' absorbed at the cut: exactly what merge re-inserts
test_eq(jd.merge_msgs(j1, j2).content, 'a\n\n\nb')  # ...so blank-line-separated content round trips byte-exactly
k1, k2 = jd.mk_message('a\n\nb', msg_type=snote).split(3)
test_eq((k1.content, k2.content), ('a', 'b'))
w1, w2 = jd.mk_message('a\n\n\nb', msg_type=snote).split(3)  # cut on the blank line: residue stays on the right
test_eq((w1.content, w2.content), ('a', '\nb'))
with expect_fail(ValueError, 'Exactly one'): jd.move_msgs(w2)

text:
Editing message text
The text editors use fastcore.tools operations on message content. Set out=True to edit a prompt’s reply Markdown instead. Assignment converts the edited reply back to an output list with prompt_output.
Other message types do not support text edits to outputs. Assign a code message’s output directly. Prompt requests and replies are separate editing targets. The former behavior that joined them for editing is no longer supported.
Pass a list of ids or 'all' for a bulk edit. The result omits unchanged messages and includes errors.
The editors inherit their signatures from fastcore.tools. doc() groups six shared replacement options under replace_params, matching fastcore.editskill:

(tdir/'edit.ipynb').write_bytes((tdir/'demo.ipynb').read_bytes())  # scratch copy: demo.ipynb stays pristine for later sections
with chdir(tdir): set_dlg('edit.ipynb')
test_eq(cur_dlg_path, (tdir/'edit.ipynb').resolve())
test_eq(cur_dlg().msg(calc.id).content, 'x = 21\nx*2')
diff = msg_str_replace(calc.id, 'x = 21', 'x = 40')
assert '-x = 21' in str(diff) and '+x = 40' in str(diff)
test_eq(read_ipynb(tdir/'edit.ipynb').msg(calc.id).content, 'x = 40\nx*2')


diff = msg_str_replace(ask.id, '**42**', '**80**', out=True)
assert '+It is **80**.' in str(diff)
test_eq(read_ipynb(tdir/'edit.ipynb').msg(ask.id).ai_res, 'It is **80**.')
assert str(msg_str_replace(calc.id, "'42'", "'80'", out=True)).startswith('error:')
assert str(msg_del_lines(setup.id, 1, 1, out=True)).startswith('error:')
bulk = msg_str_replace([setup.id, bad.id], '1/0', 'pass')
test_eq(len(bulk), 2)  # bulk mode reports errors alongside diffs
assert 'error' in bulk[0][1] and '+pass' in bulk[1][1]

Structural search
Searching for cfg = misses a binding such as cfg, aux = load(). A broad text search for a short name also finds unrelated text. Use remold’s structural queries through find_msgs(pred=...) for Python symbols and syntax.
symdef_finder finds top-level bindings. These include tuple unpacking, for, with ... as, walrus expressions, imports, and def or class definitions. symref_finder finds references to a name. ast_finder matches an ast-grep pattern.
The name queries return no matches for content that cannot parse as Python. This excludes ordinary prose in the example below:

%nbrun runs notebook code in the current kernel. Give cell ids or unique prefixes to select cells. The bare flags are above, below, all, exported, ignore_eval, continue_on_error, and show. Explicit id selections run through fastcore.nbio.run_cell with store_history=True. The kernel’s displayhook shows their results. A trailing semicolon suppresses the result through the kernel’s normal handling.

title: dialog
text:
A dialog keeps an LLM conversation in a Jupyter notebook. You can mix Markdown notes, runnable code with its outputs, and prompts with their replies. You can view, edit, diff, and version-control the conversation with notebook tools.
The format comes from Solveit, where people have used dialogs for their daily work for a couple of years. aidialog makes that format available to other tools. You can read and build dialogs, edit individual messages, and convert between dialogs and LLM chat history.
This module defines the in-memory objects: Message, Dialog, and Attachment. Later modules handle .ipynb files and chat history conversion.
from fastcore.test import *
from fastcore.nbio import mk_display, mk_error

Message types
A message has one of four types:

note contains Markdown.
code contains executable source and its Jupyter outputs.
prompt contains a user’s request and the AI’s response.
raw contains untyped text.

The file writer maps these types to notebook cells.

Identity
Messages and attachments have string ids. A dialog uses its name as its identifier. An object compares equal to another instance with the same identifier, or to the identifier itself. For example, you can check msg in dlg.messages or remove an attachment with atts.remove('img1.png').

A Message pairs a request with the answer from its addressee. For a prompt, those are the user’s request and the AI’s reply. For code, they are the source and the interpreter’s outputs. Both kinds of answer belong in output.
Notes address everyone who reads the dialog. Raw messages have no addressee. The index page explains this conversation model in more detail.
The stored fields correspond to a notebook cell: content for source, output, msg_type, id, attachments, and meta. The prompt type is an extension to the notebook cell types. Unknown metadata survives saving and loading unchanged.
A host can expose selected metadata entries as attributes through meta_attrs. This dictionary maps attribute names to metadata keys. Undeclared entries remain in meta.
New message ids contain four random bytes as hexadecimal text. The constructor converts supplied ids to strings. Hosts add display prefixes themselves, such as Solveit’s DOM _ prefix.
content, output, and msg_type use DepProp descriptors. Assigning content calls clear_inp_cache. Assigning output calls clear_out_cache. Changing the type calls both hooks and clears the output. The base class caches its AI rendering in _ai_rend. Subclasses override the hooks to clear any additional caches.
The dlg attribute refers to the owning dialog.

text:
Rendering outputs for the AI
render_outputs_ai converts Jupyter outputs to text for the model. It combines streams as a terminal would display them and removes ANSI codes. It prefers Markdown to HTML. Images don’t appear in this text because chat history sends them separately as media parts.
The renderer uses preferred_msg_out, concat_streams, and join_out from fastcore.nbio. Below, Message.render_out caches the result. Hosts can customize individual MIME conversions through Message.ai_renderers.
AI_RENDERERS defines the conversion for each preferred MIME type. It removes ANSI codes from plain text, normalizes LaTeX delimiters, and wraps JavaScript in <script> tags.
render_output_ai handles one output. render_outputs_ai handles a list. Both use preferred_msg_out to select a MIME representation. Pass renderers to override or extend the conversion table for one call. Pass dollars=True for consumers that need dollar-delimited math.

Models tend to repeat the math delimiters in their context. normalize_text_latex gives text/latex outputs consistent delimiters. It accepts bare TeX and the usual inline and display wrappers. By default, the result uses \(...\) for inline math and \[...\] for display math:

_tl(r'$$x + y$$', r'\[x + y\]')
_tl(r'$x + y$', r'\(x + y\)')

_tl(r'$$\begin{align}x &= 1\\y &= 2\end{align}$$', r'\[\begin{align}x &= 1\\y &= 2\end{align}\]')
_tl(r'\text{Price is: \$5.00}', r'\(\text{Price is: \$5.00}\)')
_tl(r'\begin{align}E = mc^2\end{align}', r'\[\begin{align}E = mc^2\end{align}\]')

_tl(r'\[x + y\]', r'$$x + y$$', dollars=True)
_tl(r'$x + y$', r'$x + y$', dollars=True)
_tl(r'\begin{align}E = mc^2\end{align}', r'$$\begin{align}E = mc^2\end{align}$$', dollars=True)
_tl(r'\text{Price is: \$5.00}', r'$\text{Price is: \$5.00}$', dollars=True)
test_eq(render_output_ai({'output_type': 'display_data', 'data': {'text/latex': '$x^2$'}}), r'\(x^2\)')
test_eq(render_output_ai({'output_type': 'display_data', 'data': {'text/latex': ['$x^', '2$']}}), r'\(x^2\)')
test_eq(render_output_ai({'output_type': 'display_data', 'data': {'text/latex': r'\(x^2\)'}}, dollars=True), '$x^2$')
test_eq(render_outputs_ai([{'output_type': 'display_data', 'data': {'text/latex': '$$x$$'}}], dollars=True), '$$x$$')

The default text/plain renderer joins lists of lines from notebook files and removes ANSI codes. A per-call renderers entry replaces that conversion:

test_eq(render_output_ai(_res({'text/plain': '\x1b[31mred\x1b[0m'})), 'red')
test_eq(render_output_ai(_res({'text/plain': ['42']}), renderers={'text/plain': lambda d: f'<{d}>'}), "<['42']>")
outs = [{'output_type': 'stream', 'name': 'stdout', 'text': 'a\n'}, {'output_type': 'stream', 'name': 'stdout', 'text': 'b\n'}, _res({'text/plain': ['42']})]

Tool block display
Solveit replies store tool calls and usage statistics in fastllm’s fenced JSON format. A json {.tool} fence contains {id, name, args, result}. A json {.usage} fence contains usage fields.
fmt_tools converts these to folded ::: details Markdown. The label comes from the block’s data and uses a code span. Solveit and viewmd convert div.details to native HTML <details> elements.
Code tools show their code and output in fences. Other tools show arguments as JSON and results in fences. A non-code tool result marked "md": true renders as Markdown instead. The emitting library uses MdStr for results that are Markdown by construction, such as a page fetch or search.
This function formats existing wire blocks. The emitting library owns their format and interpretation. fmt_tools leaves unparseable blocks unchanged.

title: dialog
text:
Running a dialog
Dialog.execute runs code messages in an execnb CaptureShell. It stores the resulting notebook-format outputs on each message in memory. Call save explicitly to write them to disk, as with other session operations.
Dialog.select_msgs chooses what to run. It uses fastcore.nbio.select_cells for ids, unique prefixes, and above and below anchors. It then keeps only messages whose msg_type is code. Prompts never execute, even though they serialize as code cells.
For messages other than explicit id selections, the cell’s eval directive determines participation. Without that directive, selection uses the notebook’s setting, then default_eval. Pass ignore_eval=True to skip this filtering. Explicitly selected code messages run regardless of eval.
d.execute(m.id, above=True) runs the selected code through m, inclusive. With no arguments, d.execute() runs all participating code messages, like Solveit’s run-all.
The returned RunResult contains the messages that ran and displays their status. You can look up messages by id.
Long reports collapse successful lines into counted markers. The report keeps the lines nearest the selection anchor: the last lines for an above run, or the first for a below run. Failures always appear with their exception name and value. The final line counts successes and failures, as %nbrun does.


source

RunResult
def RunResult(
    items:NoneType=None, head:bool=False
):
Messages run by Dialog.execute, shown as a status report


Without a shell argument, each execution call creates its own CaptureShell. Later calls do not reuse that namespace. Pass your own shell to retain variables across calls.
Every message that runs gets new outputs, including failures that replace earlier successful results. Messages that the run never reaches keep their previous outputs.

dlg2md converts a dialog to a Markdown document. Notes contribute their Markdown unchanged. Code appears in python fences, followed by outputs from this module’s render_md inside ::: output divs. Prompts and replies use ::: prompt and ::: reply divs. fmt_tools formats tool wire blocks in replies.

For document filling, exportfilter selects which messages contribute. weave uses code outputs in place of code messages. The examples below show both options.

title: msg_parts
text:
Msg and the Part subclasses describe LLM conversations without tying them to a provider. fastllm uses these types for its chat clients. Dialog libraries, transcript tools, and compaction code can use them without importing an LLM client. This module depends on fastcore.
Use mk_msg and mk_msgs to build messages from ordinary Python values. Use fmt2hist and hist2fmt to convert between messages and editable Markdown replies. The Markdown format stores tool calls, results, and usage in fenced JSON blocks.

title: msg_parts
text:
Part
A message can contain text, images, reasoning, and tool calls. Each item in Msg.content is a Part subclass. Provider converters translate between these objects and their API’s content blocks. Changing providers doesn’t require a different way to construct messages, although each provider has its own capability limits.
Subclasses register a serialization tag such as text or input_image. The tag is available as .type. Each subclass defines its own fields and display methods. Renderers call those methods without checking the tag.
Every part accepts raw and cache_control. raw retains provider details that the shared fields don’t represent, such as an Anthropic thinking signature. cache_control holds a prompt-cache directive for providers that support one. fastllm uses these parts in input coercion, response normalization, and provider serialization.
The provider APIs use different names and nesting for the same content:



API
Text
Image
File




OpenAI Responses
{"type":"input_text","text":"..."}
{"type":"input_image","image_url":"..."}
{"type":"input_file","file_data":"data:application/pdf;base64,...","filename":"..."}

{"type":"text","text":"..."}
{"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"..."}}
{"type":"file","file":{"file_data":"data:application/pdf;base64,...","filename":"..."}}

{"type":"text","text":"..."}
{"type":"image","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"image/jpeg","data":"..."}}
{"type":"document","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"application/pdf","data":"..."}}


Gemini
{"text":"..."}
{"inlineData":{"mimeType":"image/jpeg","data":"..."}}
{"fileData":{"mimeType":"application/pdf","fileUri":"..."}}



These are API representations, not constructor arguments for Part. Construct Text, InputImage, InputAudio, InputVideo, or InputFile instead. Media subclasses store a URL or data URL in text and a MIME type in mime. There is no Part.data field or provider-name override. mk_part requires the registered tag, not aliases such as image_url or pdf.

tool_text converts a tool’s return value to text for storage and provider requests. Strings pass through unchanged. Dicts and ordinary lists become JSON, not Python reprs. default=str converts values that JSON can’t encode on their own. Other objects use str.
A list containing only Part objects follows a different rule. tool_text joins their ctext values with newlines. Text remains text. Media becomes a tag such as <media input_image image/png>, matching clikernel’s kernel-image convention. fastllm uses this policy in its chat layer and provider serializers.
A stored tool block doesn’t retain media bytes or URLs. Provider converters send the media during the live turn. Reading the block later recovers the placeholder text, not the media.
Two possible lossless formats remain deferred. Embedding media in the block would enlarge stored replies with base64. Display truncation could also corrupt it. Alternatively, a ref attribute on each <media> tag could identify content in a separate store, as Solveit’s image attachments do. That would require _media_tag to write the reference and _extract_tool_parts to resolve it. Neither behavior exists yet.

title: aidialog
text:
aidialog provides the Dialog/Message model used by solveit and the fastai AI tooling ecosystem. An AI dialog is a Jupyter notebook whose cells are messages: notes, runnable code, and prompts with replies. Five modules build on each other:
Provider session files (Claude Code transcripts, Codex rollouts) and conversation compaction live in llmsurgery.

title: aidialog
text:
The theory
A dialog is a conversation between a human, an AI, and an interpreter. Each message type addresses one of them and expects a certain kind of answer:

A prompt asks the AI a question and holds its reply.
A code message gives the interpreter source and holds its outputs.
A note is read by everyone and answered by nobody.
A raw message addresses no one. It is inert matter the conversation carries along.

A reply may itself contain runnable code with results, so a whole dialog can live inside one message. reply2dlg opens a reply up as a dialog and dlg2reply puts it back.
Dialogs and Jupyter notebooks both serialize to the ipynb format, but they are not the same thing. A notebook has cells. A dialog has messages. Messages can be prompts, which notebooks cannot express, and they make structure explicit that notebooks leave implicit. E.g a heading opens a section that runs to the next heading of the same level; an export directive marks the code that belongs to a module. The shared file format means the same tools read both. The word tells you which layer you are on. File-level tools such as fastcore.nbio and exhash speak of cells and notebooks. Everything in this library speaks of messages and dialogs.
The Dialog is the center of the library. Everything else is a projection of it. A storage projection must preserve everything that means something. What it does not understand it carries verbatim in metadata, and what is broken it heals rather than rejects. A transmission projection normalizes on purpose, and what it drops is written into its contract. A display projection only goes one way. The rule is to convert in, edit at the center, and project out. The function names say the same thing. Every converter has dlg on exactly one side.

text:
Media
A model needs both the media and enough context to identify it. We put an XML <media> tag immediately before each media item. The tag records its id, type, and mime.
The ID identifies the source:

An attachment uses its UUID from the Markdown attachment:uuid reference.
A variable uses its name.
A code output image uses a content hash.

The type attribute describes where the media came from. output means a code cell output. variable means a variable value. content means media embedded in the message’s Markdown.

Media context tags
media_item accepts bytes, a MediaUrl, or a function that loads either. It checks the MIME type against the model’s capabilities before preparing the data. Successful results contain the <media> tag followed by the data.
The capability flags are supports_vision, supports_video_input, supports_pdf_input, and supports_audio_input. A missing flag means no support for that media type. The unsupported-media message asks the user to choose a model that supports it.
Expected failures return a <media-unavailable> tag. These include missing files, invalid base64, and unavailable or unsupported data. The tag records the reason and tells the model to inform the user that it cannot see the media. Image preparation and a host’s path checks can also report these failures. Unexpected exceptions still propagate.

PDF token estimates use a page count. pdf_pages reads /Count values from /Pages nodes without a PDF library. In a complete page tree, the root holds the total and no child has a larger count. The function takes the largest count it finds.
PDF 1.5 permits these nodes inside compressed object streams. pdf_pages uses zlib to inspect those streams too. An incremental edit that removes pages can leave an older, larger root in the file. Counting that root overestimates the token budget rather than underestimating it. This is a heuristic, not a complete PDF parser. It returns zero when it finds no matching count.


source

pdf_pages
def pdf_pages(
    b:bytes
):
Page count of PDF b: the largest /Count on a /Pages node, in the clear or inside an inflated object stream


These hand-built PDFs contain the same page tree, once uncompressed and once in a compressed object stream:

def _pdf(objs): return b'%PDF-1.5\n' + b''.join(f'{i} 0 obj\n'.encode()+o+b'\nendobj\n' for i,o in enumerate(objs, 1)) + b'%%EOF'
pages = b'<< /Type /Pages /Count 3 /Kids [3 0 R 4 0 R 5 0 R] >>'
kids = [b'<< /Type /Page /Parent 2 0 R >>']*3
plain = _pdf([b'<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>', pages, *kids])
packed = zlib.compress(b'2 0 ' + pages)
objstm = _pdf([b'<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>', b'<< /Type /ObjStm /N 1 /First 4 /Filter /FlateDecode /Length %d >>\nstream\n' % len(packed) + packed + b'\nendstream', *kids])
test_eq((pdf_pages(plain), pdf_pages(objstm), pdf_pages(b'%PDF-1.5\n%%EOF')), (3, 3, 0))
pdf_pages(objstm)

Static media refs
Add #ai to a Markdown image target to include it in model context: ![alt](ref#ai). The model doesn’t see media from links without this suffix.
The target can be an http:// or https:// URL, a data: URL, or a file path. Web URLs use a lazy MediaUrl. Data URLs decode inline. Dialog.media_path resolves file paths.
Hosts patch media_path to apply their own directories and safety rules. Solveit uses it to map /static/ and restrict production access to its data directory.

Resolve a file reference to an absolute path. Hosts can override path and safety rules.

tdir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()).resolve()

Sigil refs and variables
Prompts can refer to kernel values, tools, and shell output with a character before a backtick expression:

$`expr` requests the value of a kernel expression.
&`tool` activates a tool.
!`cmd` requests shell output in hosts that provide a shell.

This module parses the references. The host evaluates them because it owns the kernel, toolset, and shell.
get_refs parses names for the & form. It accepts a single name or a list such as &`[python, bash]`. sigil_pat handles $ and !. Their backtick content can be an expression or command, rather than a name.


source

get_refs
def get_refs(
    cts, sigil:str='&'
):
Return sorted unique names referenced via sigilname or sigil[name, name] pattern in msgs



test_eq(get_refs('use &`bash` and &`[python, bash]`'), ['bash', 'python'])
test_eq(get_refs('dotted names too: &`np.load`'), ['np.load'])
test_is(get_refs('no refs here, and no $`vars` either'), None)

get_exprs collects references from prompt content. expr_mtypes defines the participating message types. Notes, code, and outputs don’t request interpolation, even when they contain the same syntax. Pass sigil='!' to collect shell references instead of kernel expressions. Parsing doesn’t evaluate either kind of reference.


source

get_exprs
def get_exprs(
    msgs, sigil:str='$'
):
Sorted unique refs of sigil form found in prompt messages of msgs




source

sigil_pat
def sigil_pat(
    sigil
):
Regex for sigilpayload refs, e.g. $expr or !cmd



test_eq(expr_pat.findall('$`myvar`'), ['myvar'])
test_eq(expr_pat.findall('$`now()`'), ['now()'])
test_eq(expr_pat.findall('$`add(1, 2)`'), ['add(1, 2)'])
test_eq(expr_pat.findall('$`[obj.attr, d["key"], fn(*args,**kws)]`'), ['[obj.attr, d["key"], fn(*args,**kws)]'])
test_eq(expr_pat.findall('Check $`x` and $`f(y)`'), ['x', 'f(y)'])

References in notes and code stay out of the result. Repeating a reference in prompts adds no duplicate:

raw = [mk('prompt', '>hello $`x`'), mk('note', '$`not_variable1`'), mk('code', output="aaa", content="'$`not_variable2`'"),
    mk('prompt', 'hi <hi $`y`'), mk('prompt', '$`x`, $`y`')]
test_eq(get_exprs(raw), ['x', 'y'])
raw += [mk('prompt', 'run !`ls -la` and !`git status`'), mk('note', '!`not_a_cmd`')]
test_eq(get_exprs(raw, sigil='!'), ['git status', 'ls -la'])
test_eq(get_exprs(raw), ['x', 'y'])  # the default is unaffected by ! refs

After evaluation, the host supplies a dictionary mapping each reference to its value. vars_tag prepares those values for context. Ordinary values go in a <variables> element made with fastcore’s Variables and Variable components. Recognized media values go in separate media parts.


source

vars_tag
def vars_tag(
    aim_info, ns:NoneType=None
):
 element and byte variables for this message



imns = dict(img=_mk_img(_imgb64), x=4, y=3, img2=_mk_img(_imgb64))
vt = vars_tag(dict(supports_vision=True), imns)
test_eq(to_xml(vt['vars_tag']), '''<variables>The 'variables' section provides values of: $`img`, $`x`, $`y`, $`img2`<variable name="x" type="int">4</variable><variable name="y" type="int">3</variable></variables>''')

Media variables use alternating tags and bytes. Images, audio, and video can all go in a mk_msgs content list this way:

test_eq(len(vt['vars_bytes']), 4)
test_eq(vt['vars_bytes'][0], '<media id="img" type="variable" mime="image/png"></media>')
test_eq(vt['vars_bytes'][2], '<media id="img2" type="variable" mime="image/png"></media>')

Shell results use the full !`cmd` reference as their variable name. vars_tag keeps that spelling in the introductory text and the variable tag. Shell results share the same section and position as other variables:

vt = vars_tag({}, {'x': 4, '!`ls -la`': 'total 0'})
test_eq(to_xml(vt['vars_tag']), '''<variables>The 'variables' section provides values of: $`x`, !`ls -la`<variable name="x" type="int">4</variable><variable name="!`ls -la`" type="str">total 0</variable></variables>''')

vars_hist returns one user turn containing the namespace and an assistant acknowledgement. Hosts prepend this exchange to history. Variable values then appear once at a stable position for caching. An empty namespace produces no exchange:

vars_hist
def vars_hist(
    aim_info, ns:NoneType=None
):
Single history turn holding all variable values, to sit above everything else



test_eq(vars_hist({}, {}), [])
test_eq(vars_hist({}, None), [])
vh = vars_hist({}, {'x': 4, 'y': 3})
test_eq(len(vh), 2)
test_eq(vh[0][0], """<variables>The 'variables' section provides values of: $`x`, $`y`<variable name="x" type="int">4</variable><variable name="y" type="int">3</variable></variables>""")
vh = vars_hist(dict(supports_vision=True), {'img': _mk_img(_imgb64), 'x': 4})
test_eq(len(vh[0]), 3)
test_eq(vh[0][1], '<media id="img" type="variable" mime="image/png"></media>')

Hosts evaluate references in their kernels with ipyfuncs’ eval_exprs, usually through a client helper. Each requested expression has a result. Evaluation failures return an <error> element as a string instead of omitting the key. Its type attribute identifies the exception.
is_nameerr recognizes the NameError marker. Hosts use it to warn about missing variables rather than show the error as a variable value. Other errors remain visible in the values. This distinguishes a missing name from a reference whose evaluation failed.

Message XML Helpers
Message.hist_xml formats notes, code, and other non-prompt messages with item2xml. The tag names the message type and contains the content directly. An <out> section contains any output. This history rendering includes time information. Message.to_xml provides the concise rendering used by dlgskill.
Prompts use prompt_txt instead. The AI reply belongs to the next history turn, not inside the prompt XML.

The prompt envelope
A user turn can contain notes, code, and media before the prompt. task_tags separates the actual request from that context. It returns an <instructions> element followed by a <prompt> element containing the request.
The prompt’s sid identifies the message for tools. Its time records the local run time when available. prompt_txt uses the dialog’s timezone, or UTC without one.
Hosts can add warnings alongside the live prompt. warning_tag puts these in a <system-reminder> element. Examples include undefined variables and context-budget trims.

text:
Dialogs to canonical messages
dlg2chat converts a dialog into the canonical Msg format used for provider conversions and transcript editing. It first calls dlg2hist to group the user turns. reply2chat then parses each stored reply with msg_parts.fmt2hist and separates its tool calls and results. You can also use reply2chat on a single reply string.
The dialog must end with a prompt. dlg2chat rejects duplicate tool-call IDs, including duplicates in hand-authored replies. By default, prompts include the solveit serving envelope from task_tags. For transcript reconstruction, pass plain=True to keep the prompt’s bare content.
This conversion does not preserve every part of a stored reply. fmt2hist removes thinking blocks. reply2dlg and dlg2reply have the same limitation. Keep the original reply string if you need those blocks.


source

reply2chat
def reply2chat(
    outp:str
)->list[aidialog.msg_parts.Msg]:
Chat messages for a stored reply: fmt2hist-parsed parts in strict call/result alternation




source

dlg2chat
def dlg2chat(
    dlg, # A `Dialog`, ending with a prompt
    aim_info:NoneType=None, # Model capability dict for media handling; images enabled if None
    plain:bool=False, # Render prompts as bare content, without the serving envelope?
):
Canonical chat messages for dlg, with each reply’s tool calls recovered as real parts


We’ll build a reply containing a tool-call details block in the stored reply format:

def _mk_dtl(func, args, result, tid='x1'):
    d = json.dumps(dict(id=tid, name=func, args=args, result=result))
    return f"```json {{.tool}}\n{d}\n```"

py_dtl = _mk_dtl('python', {'code':'1+1'}, '2')


ddlg = Dialog(name='canon')
ddlg.mk_message('What is 1+1?', msg_type=sprompt, output=f"Check:\n\n{py_dtl}\n\nIt is 2.")
cm = dlg2chat(ddlg)
test_eq([m.role for m in cm], ['user', 'assistant', 'tool', 'assistant'])
test_eq(cm[1].content[1].name, 'python')

A reply can contain sequential tool calls, each using the previous result. fmt2hist groups these into an assistant message and a tool-result message. dlg2chat separates them again into call/result pairs in order. This matches the sequence that live sessions record without presenting the calls as parallel:

py_dtl2 = _mk_dtl('python', {'code':'2+2'}, '4', 'x2')
sdlg = Dialog(name='seq')
sdlg.mk_message('Two steps.', msg_type=sprompt, output=f"{py_dtl}\n\n{py_dtl2}\n\nDone.")
sm = dlg2chat(sdlg)
test_eq([(m.role, len(m.content)) for m in sm], [('user',1), ('assistant',1), ('tool',1), ('assistant',1), ('tool',1), ('assistant',1)])
test_eq(sm[2].content[0].id, sm[1].content[0].id)
test_eq(sm[4].content[0].id, sm[3].content[0].id)


bad = Dialog(name='dup')
bad.mk_message('a', msg_type=sprompt, output=py_dtl)
bad.mk_message('b', msg_type=sprompt, output=py_dtl)
with expect_fail(ValueError, 'duplicate tool call id'): dlg2chat(bad)

chat2dlg creates one prompt per user turn. It renders the assistant and tool messages into that prompt’s reply with hist2fmt. User images become attachments with references in the question text.
hist2fmt writes tool calls and results as fenced JSON. The round-trip checks below compare canonical messages rather than the original Markdown. Its mx limit truncates tool results and permits string arguments up to five times that length. Use mx=None to disable these limits for matched call/result pairs. Server calls without separate results still use their default display limit.
chat2dlg removes the prompt envelope and keeps the request text. An envelope’s sid restores the original message ID. Converting the reconstructed dialog back to chat then restores that ID in the envelope.


source

chat2dlg
def chat2dlg(
    msgs, # Canonical messages, e.g. from `dlg2chat`
    name, # Dialog name
    cls:type=Dialog, # Dialog class to create
    mx:int=2000, # Maximum characters per rendered tool input/output string; None disables truncation (see `hist2fmt`)
):
Convert canonical messages to a dialog with one prompt per user turn.



rdlg = chat2dlg(dlg2chat(sdlg), 'seq round-trip')
test_eq(len(rdlg.messages), 1)
test_eq(rdlg.messages[0].content, 'Two steps.')
test_eq(dlg2chat(rdlg), sm)

Producers can attach provenance to a Msg with a dynamic meta attribute. It isn’t a class field. For example, recs2chat and items2chat record the source’s created time and uid there.
chat2dlg copies each user message’s metadata to its dialog message. It derives an eight-hex-digit ID from the uid. Repeating the conversion preserves these IDs and the link to the source record. An embedded solveit sid takes precedence:

mm = mk_msg('When was this?')
mm.meta = dict(created='2026-07-09T00:26:40.000Z', uid='abc-123')
mdlg = chat2dlg([mm, Msg('assistant', [Text('July 9.')])], 'meta')
m0 = mdlg.messages[0]
test_eq(m0.meta, mm.meta)
test_eq(m0.id, hashlib.md5(b'abc-123').hexdigest()[:8])
m0.meta

{'created': '2026-07-09T00:26:40.000Z', 'uid': 'abc-123'}


Without a provenance uid, chat2dlg derives the ID from the dialog name and turn position. Repeating the conversion with the same name and turns gives the same IDs:

d1,d2 = chat2dlg([mk_msg('a'), Msg('assistant', [Text('b')])], 'same'), chat2dlg([mk_msg('a'), Msg('assistant', [Text('b')])], 'same')
test_eq(d1.messages[0].id, d2.messages[0].id)

A continuation transcript can start with assistant messages when earlier turns are in a predecessor file. chat2dlg puts these replies on an empty first prompt instead of raising an error:

fdlg = chat2dlg([Msg('assistant', [Text('...continuing.')]), mk_msg('And then?'), Msg('assistant', [Text('Done.')])], 'cont')
test_eq(len(fdlg.messages), 2)
test_eq(fdlg.messages[0].content, '')
assert '...continuing.' in fdlg.messages[0].ai_res
fdlg.summary()

Notes and code before a prompt join that prompt’s user turn. This dialog shows prompts with and without preceding context, plus an empty AI response. The image questions are plain text here; the media examples above show how to attach the images themselves:

raw = [

    mk('note', 'a note between turns'),
    mk('code', output="aaa", content="'some source text'"),

title: hist
text:
Reply sub-dialogs
A prompt stores its AI reply as Markdown with fenced JSON tool blocks. Convert legacy HTML details blocks with conv_tools before parsing them. Use reply2dlg to turn a reply into a dialog of notes and code messages. You can then edit it with the usual message operations. dlg2reply converts the edited dialog back to reply Markdown.
reply2dlg parses through fmt2hist. That parser removes token-usage and thinking blocks. When the reply ends with tool results, it adds a final . note to avoid empty assistant text. These changes also occur when converting replies to chat history.
fmt2hist retains server-tool calls. reply2dlg converts them to code messages too, but the sub-dialog does not retain their server flag.


source

reply2dlg
def reply2dlg(
    pmsg
):
Explode pmsg’s AI reply into a Dialog of note and code messages


reply2dlg writes each tool call as Python source with repr values for the keyword arguments. The source is the sole record of the tool name and arguments. Later, ast parses them back without executing the call. The output list holds the result. The message’s meta['tool_id'] holds the call ID.
Here’s a reply containing prose, a Python tool call, and its result. We’ll turn it into a sub-dialog, edit the call’s argument, and convert it back:

tu1 = ToolUse(id='x1', name='python', arguments={'code':'1+1'})
tr1 = ToolResult(id='x1', name='python', text='2')
rmsgs = [Msg(role='assistant', content=[Text('Check:'), tu1]), Msg(role='tool', content=[tr1]),
    Msg(role='assistant', content=[Text('It is 2.')])]
pm = Message('What is 1+1?', msg_type=sprompt, output=hist2fmt(rmsgs, mx=None))
Markdown(pm.ai_res)

Check:
{
  "id": "x1",
  "name": "python",
  "args": {
    "code": "1+1"
  },
  "result": "2"
}
It is 2.



sub = reply2dlg(pm)
sub

4340d65d


Check:
python(code=‘1+1’) ⇒ [{‘output_type’: ‘execute_result’, ‘metadata’: {}, ‘data’: …
It is 2.





test_eq([m.msg_type for m in sub.messages], [snote, scode, snote])
test_eq(sub.messages[1].content, "python(code='1+1')")
test_eq(sub.messages[1].output, code_output('2'))
test_eq(sub.messages[1].meta['tool_id'], 'x1')
sub.messages[1]

8a814699:c:python(code=‘1+1’) ⇒ out(102)


Dotted tool names such as tools.write_stdin remain valid Python calls. The resulting code message can run in an environment that provides the tool:

dtc = ToolUse('d1', 'tools.write_stdin', {'session_id':7, 'chars':'x'})
dpm = Message('Continue.', msg_type=sprompt, output=hist2fmt(
    [Msg(role='assistant', content=[dtc]), mk_tool_res_msg([dtc], ['ok']), Msg(role='assistant', content=[Text('Done.')])], mx=None))
dsub = reply2dlg(dpm)
test_eq(dsub.messages[0].content, "tools.write_stdin(session_id=7, chars='x')")
dsub.messages[0].content

"tools.write_stdin(session_id=7, chars='x')"


dlg2reply converts code messages to fenced JSON tool blocks with mk_tr_details, without truncation. Each block records the call ID, name, arguments, and result. Notes keep their text apart from surrounding whitespace. The function joins the nonempty blocks with blank lines.
For replies already in the normalized hist2fmt format, these examples round-trip exactly:


source

dlg2reply
def dlg2reply(
    sub
):
Implode a sub-dialog of note and code messages back into reply markdown



test_eq(dlg2reply(sub), pm.ai_res)
test_eq(dlg2reply(dsub), dpm.ai_res)

Changing a keyword argument in the source changes that argument in the reply. The call keeps its ID:

sub.messages[1].content = "python(code='1+2')"
tu = first(p for m in fmt2hist(dlg2reply(sub)) for p in m.content if isinstance(p, ToolUse))
test_eq(tu.arguments, {'code':'1+2'})
test_eq(tu.id, 'x1')



source

Message.tool_call
def tool_call():
Parsed dict(name=..., arguments=...) when this code message’s source is a literal tool call, else None


For UIs and review code, tool_call reads the name and arguments without generating an ID or changing the message. It returns None for a note or source that isn’t a keyword-only call expression. Argument values must be Python literals. Nonliteral values raise during parsing:

test_eq(sub.messages[1].tool_call, dict(name='python', arguments={'code':'1+2'}))
test_eq(sub.messages[0].tool_call, None)  # a note
test_eq(Message('x = 1', msg_type=scode).tool_call, None)  # not a call expression

Parallel tool calls appear as adjacent tool blocks in a stored reply. reply2dlg makes one code message per call in document order. The final . note comes from fmt2hist. Converting this reply to a sub-dialog and back preserves the history from dlg2chat:

tus = [ToolUse(id=f'x{i}', name='simple_add', arguments=dict(a=i, b=1)) for i in (2,3,4)]
tres = [ToolResult(id=f'x{i}', name='simple_add', text=str(i+1)) for i in (2,3,4)]
vmsgs = [Msg(role='assistant', content=[Text('Adding.'), *tus]), Msg(role='tool', content=tres)]
vdlg = Dialog(name='volley')
vpm = vdlg.mk_message('Add some numbers.', msg_type=sprompt, output=hist2fmt(vmsgs, mx=None))
vsub = reply2dlg(vpm)
test_eq([m.msg_type for m in vsub.messages], [snote, scode, scode, scode, snote])


v2 = Dialog(name='volley2')
v2.mk_message('Add some numbers.', msg_type=sprompt, output=dlg2reply(vsub), id=vpm.id)
test_eq(dlg2chat(v2), dlg2chat(vdlg))

You can insert new notes and calls into the sub-dialog. dlg2reply includes them in the reply and assigns IDs to calls that don’t have one. The example checks that the IDs are distinct:

vsub.mk_message('One more:', msg_type=snote)
nc = vsub.mk_message('simple_add(a=5, b=1)', output=code_output('6'))
r3 = dlg2reply(vsub)
assert 'One more:' in r3
ids = [p.id for m in fmt2hist(r3) for p in m.content if isinstance(p, ToolUse)]
test_eq(len(ids), len(set(ids)))
assert nc.meta['tool_id']

A reply without tool calls becomes one note. reply2dlg raises ValueError for a tool name that isn’t a dotted Python identifier. dlg2reply raises for code that isn’t a keyword-only tool call:

sub1 = reply2dlg(Message('hi', msg_type=sprompt, output='Just prose.'))
test_eq([m.msg_type for m in sub1.messages], [snote])
test_eq(dlg2reply(sub1), 'Just prose.')


badp = [Msg(role='assistant', content=[ToolUse(id='b1', name='foo-bar')]),
    Msg(role='tool', content=[ToolResult(id='b1', name='foo-bar', text='x')])]
with expect_fail(ValueError, 'identifier'): reply2dlg(Message('p', msg_type=sprompt, output=hist2fmt(badp, mx=None)))
with expect_fail(ValueError, 'tool call'): dlg2reply(Dialog(name='b', messages=[Message('1+1', msg_type=scode)]))

Every message type supports attachments, but nbformat permits cell attachments only on markdown and raw cells. For code cells, aidialog follows rustygate’s convention: store attachments in notebook metadata under metadata.attachments[cell_id]. Rustygate calls this location the attachment home.
home_atts moves code-cell attachments there before writing. unhome_atts restores them to their cells before reading. This matches rustygate’s files and the ordinary cell representation its API returns. In memory, use Message.attachments regardless of the message type.

Store code-cell attachments in notebook metadata using rustygate’s convention


A prompt contains both a question and an AI reply. to_cell writes it as a code cell with solveit_ai: true in metadata. The source starts with %%prompt, followed by the question. The reply uses the display_data output from prompt_output, with is_ai_res in its metadata.
Outside Solveit, a runner without the %%prompt magic raises UsageError rather than trying to execute the question as Python. A host can define that magic to run prompts. cell2msg removes the magic line when reconstructing the message.

Message.cell_meta
def cell_meta():
Build cell metadata from meta and declared attributes, omitting falsy attribute values


to_cell calls cell_meta to prepare the cell’s metadata. Override cell_meta when your host uses different types in memory and on disk. Call super() first, then convert the values it returns. For example, Solveit uses integer UI flags, but the notebook schema requires booleans for collapsed and hide_input.

    version:int=2
):
Convert message to a notebook cell



om = Message('x', msg_type='code', output=[dict(output_type='execute_result', data={'text/plain':'42'}, metadata={'__type':'Safe'}, execution_count=1)])

test_eq(om.output[0]['metadata'], {'__type':'Safe'})  # ...and serializing never mutates the live output (hosts read it after writes)


test_eq(Message().to_cell()['metadata'],{})

meta_attrs maps attributes on a message to metadata keys in its notebook cell. cell_meta writes those attributes to their declared keys. It omits falsy attribute values. cell2msg restores the attributes when reading.
The Message constructor also extracts declared attributes from meta=. An attribute’s default cannot hide a value supplied in that metadata. Keys outside meta_attrs remain in Message.meta and round-trip unchanged.
Here a host adds a bookmark attribute to its message class.

class NoteMsg(Message): meta_attrs = dict(bookmark='bookmark')
class NoteDlg(Dialog): msg_cls = NoteMsg

test_eq(NoteMsg('x', meta=dict(bookmark=7)).to_cell()['metadata'], {'bookmark': 7})  # ...so it round-trips to the file

class FlagMsg(Message):
    meta_attrs = dict(collapsed='collapsed')

assert FlagMsg(collapsed=1).to_cell()['metadata']['collapsed'] is True

def save(
    fname:NoneType=None
):
Write back to fname, or to the path_ stamped by read_ipynb


read_ipynb records the source file in dlg.path_. You can edit the dialog and call save() without passing the path again. The trailing underscore distinguishes this working attribute from a host’s own path property.
read_ipynb and file writes through write_ipynb record the file’s safe_mtime in dlg.mtime_. A host can compare that timestamp with the current file timestamp when checking for external writes. A new dialog has None for both attributes. save() needs an explicit filename until the dialog has a path_.
The file below already uses aidialog’s normalized format. Saving it without edits preserves its bytes, although the save still updates the file’s timestamp.

before = (tstdir/'dlg.ipynb').read_text()
dlg.save()
test_eq((tstdir/'dlg.ipynb').read_text(), before)
test_eq(dlg.mtime_, dlg.path_.stat().st_mtime)
assert isinstance(dlg.messages, Msgs)
unread = Dialog(name='unread')
test_eq((unread.path_, unread.mtime_), (None,None))
with expect_fail(ValueError, 'path_'): unread.save()


Metadata preservation
The base Message class declares two metadata attributes. skipped hides a message from AI context. pinned keeps it through context eviction. Both use Solveit’s literal metadata keys for compatibility between hosts.
Other application metadata remains in Message.meta unless a subclass declares it in meta_attrs. Notebook-level application metadata remains in Dialog.meta. The plain classes preserve those annotations when reading and writing files from another host.

m0 = dlg.messages[0]
m0.meta['my_app_flag'] = dict(level=3)
dlg.meta['my_app'] = dict(version=1)
dlg.write(tstdir)
dlg = read_ipynb(tstdir/'dlg')
test_eq(dlg.messages[0].meta['my_app_flag'], dict(level=3))
test_eq(dlg.meta['my_app'], dict(version=1))

Set skipped and pinned as message attributes. Saving writes truthy values to their metadata keys. Reading restores them as attributes and removes those keys from Message.meta. Unset or falsy attributes add no metadata to the file.

m0 = dlg.messages[0]
m0.skipped = 1
m0.pinned = True
dlg.write(tstdir)
rt = read_ipynb(tstdir/'dlg')
test_eq(rt.messages[0].skipped, 1)                  # promoted back as a real attribute
test_eq(rt.messages[0].pinned, True)
assert 'skipped' not in rt.messages[0].meta         # claimed by meta_attrs, so not left in meta
test_eq(rt.messages[1].skipped, 0)                  # untouched message: class default, and
assert 'skipped' not in rt.messages[1].cell_meta()  # ...falsy means nothing written to the file



Round-trip fidelity
write_ipynb normalizes notebooks. For example, it writes null for each code cell’s execution count, even if that cell has run. The first save can therefore change the input file without changing its source or displayed output.
After normalization, reading and writing an unedited dialog produces identical JSON with this serializer. Changes in that JSON indicate changes to the serialized dialog. Other notebook tools can still change formatting or serialization without changing the message content.
We check this property against the repository’s notebooks as well as the constructed examples.

for p in sorted(Path('.').glob('0*.ipynb')):
    s = write_ipynb(read_ipynb(str(p)))
    test_eq(write_ipynb(reads_ipynb(s)), s)

Hand-edited notebooks can contain fields that nbformat rejects. This example reproduces a real file’s stray outputs key on a markdown cell. read_ipynb calls repair_nb before constructing messages. The repaired notebook keeps the source text and omits the invalid key. Writing it produces a file that passes validation.

bad_cells = [dict(cell_type='markdown', id='aaaa1111', metadata={}, source='hi', outputs=[])]
(tstdir/'bad.ipynb').write_text(json.dumps(dict(nbformat=4, nbformat_minor=5, metadata={}, cells=bad_cells)))
with expect_fail(NotebookValidationError): nbformat.validate(nbformat.read(tstdir/'bad.ipynb', as_version=4))
healed = write_ipynb(read_ipynb(tstdir/'bad'))
nbformat.validate(nbformat.reads(healed, as_version=4))
assert 'hi' in healed

conv_old_prompts converts old markdown prompt cells to the current code-cell format. It changes the supplied notebook object in place and returns the changed cell ids. A host can use that list to decide whether to write the file back after opening it.

def conv_old_prompts(
    nb
):
Convert old markdown prompt cells to code cells in place and return their changed ids


Old prompt cells use markdown with solveit_ai metadata. Their source contains the question and reply separated by _reply_sep. Current writers use code cells instead.
The example builds an old prompt using that separator. Conversion preserves its question, reply, and attachment. The new notebook passes schema validation and reconstructs the same message when read.

onb = dict(nbformat=4, nbformat_minor=5, metadata={}, cells=[dict(
    cell_type='markdown', id='opr1', metadata=dict(solveit_ai=True),
    source='What is 7*6?' + _reply_sep + '**42**.',
    attachments={'att1': {'image/png': 'bm90IHJlYWxseSBhIHBuZw=='}})])
test_eq(conv_old_prompts(onb), ['opr1'])
ocell = onb['cells'][0]
test_eq((ocell['cell_type'], ocell['source']), ('code', '%%prompt\nWhat is 7*6?'))
assert 'attachments' not in ocell                # the retype homed the attachment
nbformat.validate(nbformat.from_dict(onb))
test_eq(conv_old_prompts(onb), [])               # converted cells no longer match: idempotent
back = reads_ipynb(json.dumps(onb)).messages[0]
test_eq((back.content, back.ai_res), ('What is 7*6?', '**42**.'))
test_eq(back.attachments[0].data, b'not really a png')
